claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain relative to pure tungsten at high temperature.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved toughness relative to pure tungsten at high temperature.
The multi-principal-element design of WTaTiVZr promotes grain refinement.
The multi-principal-element design of WTaTiVZr promotes formation of coherent Zr-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Zr-rich precipitates occur particularly at or near grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
Fine grains and Zr-rich precipitates impede dislocation motion.
The fine grains and precipitates produce a more uniform distribution of plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays localized failure.
Grain-boundary precipitates mitigate crack propagation under cyclic and high-temperature loading.
Standard processing such as casting followed by annealing produces a homogeneous, refined-grain WTaTiVZr microstructure.
Commercially processed pure tungsten has coarser grains than the proposed WTaTiVZr material.
Commercially processed pure tungsten lacks the Zr-rich dispersion-strengthening precipitates proposed for WTaTiVZr.
At 1200–1300°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain to failure than pure tungsten.
At 1200–1300°C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit higher fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanical improvement will correlate with fine grains and coherent Zr-rich precipitates.
Approximately 1200–1300°C is a temperature range relevant to plasma-facing-component service.
At significantly lower temperatures, the precipitates may have a weaker influence on dislocation dynamics and crack blunting.
At significantly lower temperatures, the precipitates may behave in a brittle manner.

contradictions.description: The initial-state comparison specifies cast/annealed WTaTiVZr versus commercially processed pure tungsten, whereas the intervention and falsification design say the materials are processed under identical conditions. These are materially different control definitions.
